## Summary

**Background.** Post-transplant cyclophosphamide (PTCy) is used for
graft-versus-host disease (GVHD) prophylaxis after allogeneic
haematopoietic stem-cell transplantation (allo-HSCT), but its impact on
infection risk versus longer-established prophylaxis regimens has not
been systematically quantified. We evaluated infection outcomes
alongside survival, relapse and non-relapse mortality, and GVHD.

**Methods.** In this systematic review and Bayesian meta-analysis, we
searched EMBASE, PubMed, and SCOPUS from inception to April 30, 2026 for
studies comparing PTCy-based GVHD prophylaxis with alternative regimens
in adult allo-HSCT recipients. Comparisons were pre-specified: PTCy
versus calcineurin inhibitor (CNI) plus methotrexate or mycophenolate
(C1); PTCy versus anti-thymocyte globulin (ATG; C2); and within-PTCy
regimen variants (C3). Outcomes were overall survival (OS; primary),
non-relapse mortality (NRM), acute GVHD grade II–IV, CMV reactivation,
bloodstream infection (BSI), and invasive fungal infection (IFI). We
fitted Bayesian random-effects binomial-logistic models. PROSPERO
registration: CRD420261372156.

**Findings.** Of 4145 records, 251 studies (525 arms; 178 146 patients)
were included, 106 in the meta-analysis. In C1 (73 studies), PTCy
was associated with better OS (odds ratio 0·76 \[95% credible interval 0·62–0·93\]) and
less acute GVHD (0·58 \[0·44–0·77\]); CMV and BSI estimates were
elevated but imprecise (1·22 \[0·90–1·65\]; 1·42 \[0·57–2·98\], the
latter from six studies). In C2
(27 studies), OS favoured PTCy versus ATG (0·75 \[0·42–1·31\];
imprecise) and CMV did not differ (0·86 \[0·50–1·42\]). The
CMV estimate was larger post-2020 (1·46
\[1·01–2·05\]). GRADE certainty was
very low for all outcomes.

**Interpretation.** PTCy is associated with better survival and less GVHD versus
CNI-based prophylaxis, with uncertain benefit versus ATG. Infection
estimates were compatible with increased CMV and bacterial risk versus
less T-cell-depleting regimens, but wide. CMV direction fits a class
effect of T-cell depletion, whereas BK virus elevation was
comparator-invariant, suggesting a cyclophosphamide-specific effect;
both readings are hypothesis-generating.

**Funding.** There was no funding source for this study.

## Research in context

::: panel
### Evidence before this study

We searched PubMed, EMBASE and SCOPUS for systematic reviews and
meta-analyses of post-transplant cyclophosphamide in allogeneic
haematopoietic stem-cell transplantation published from database
inception to June 1, 2026, using the terms "post-transplant
cyclophosphamide" AND ("meta-analysis" OR "systematic review"). We
identified six comparative meta-analyses [@gagelmann2019; @jin2026;
@arcuri2019; @arcuri2021; @tang2023; @luo2025] encompassing 6–20 studies
each. All evaluated survival and GVHD outcomes; only two [@jin2026;
@tang2023] pooled infection outcomes, each with 2–4 studies per
infection type. No prior meta-analysis simultaneously evaluated CMV,
bacterial, and fungal infections alongside survival and GVHD. No prior
study compared PTCy against both CNI-based and ATG-based comparators in
a unified framework, and none has proposed a mechanistic explanation for
the apparently contradictory infection findings across comparator
contexts.

### Added value of this study

In this large systematic review and meta-analysis (251 studies, 178 146
patients), we were able to systematically pool CMV, bloodstream
infection, and invasive fungal infection risk in the context of GVHD and
survival within the same analytic framework. Its dual-comparator design
shows that the estimated effect of PTCy on CMV reverses direction
depending on the comparator's own T-cell depletion depth, although the
contrast is indirect and not formally resolved. Elevated average infection
risk was estimated versus CNI-based (odds ratio 1·22 \[0·90–1·65\]) but
not ATG-based (0·86 \[0·50–1·42\]) prophylaxis, a directional pattern
compatible with — but not establishing — a T-cell depletion-depth
gradient: a formal meta-regression on comparator class did not
resolve the difference (ratio of odds ratios 0·71 \[0·41–1·20\];
appendix S9).

### Implications of all the available evidence

PTCy is associated with better overall survival and less GVHD across
comparator types, although certainty of evidence is very low
throughout. Infection estimates are imprecise and pattern differently
by pathogen: CMV estimates are directionally consistent with the
comparator's T-cell depletion depth without establishing it, whereas
BK virus elevation appears cyclophosphamide-specific. Clinical
strategies to mitigate these risks should target T-cell reconstitution
(adoptive T-cell therapy, optimised letermovir prophylaxis, earlier
immunosuppression tapering) rather than PTCy avoidance. Within-PTCy
regimen variants show no detectable differences, but with k = 4–7 per
outcome this is absence of evidence, not evidence of equivalence.
:::

## Introduction

Post-transplant cyclophosphamide (PTCy) has transformed the practice of
allogeneic haematopoietic stem-cell transplantation (allo-HSCT) by
enabling safe transplantation across HLA barriers and simplifying
graft-versus-host disease (GVHD) prophylaxis.[@odonnell2002] Originally
developed for haploidentical transplantation[@luznik2008], PTCy is now
widely used across all donor types[@kanakry2016] and the BMT CTN
1703/1801 randomised controlled trial (RCT) established its superiority
over conventional calcineurin inhibitor (CNI)-based prophylaxis for
GVHD-free, relapse-free survival.[@bolanosmeade2023]

Uncertainty remains regarding the magnitude of PTCy on infection risk
after transplant. Compared to CNI-based prophylaxis, CIBMTR registry
studies have reported that PTCy-based regimens are associated with
increased cytomegalovirus (CMV) reactivation[@goldsmith2021] and a
higher incidence of bacterial bloodstream infections with comparable or
reduced rates of fungal infections.[@papanicolaou2024]. This excess
risk, however, has been difficult to quantify overall because prior
meta-analyses have been restricted to single comparisons, limited to
6–20 studies, and have rarely included infection as a primary outcome.
The absence of a unified analytic framework spanning multiple comparator
contexts raises a fundamental question: are infection risks attributable
to PTCy itself, or to the depth of T-cell depletion inherent to any
intensive GVHD prophylaxis ? Answering this question requires
simultaneous comparison of PTCy against both less depleting (CNI plus
methotrexate) and more depleting (anti-thymocyte globulin \[ATG\])
regimens

To address this question, we conducted a systematic review and Bayesian
meta-analysis to simultaneously evaluate survival, GVHD, and infection
outcomes of PTCy-based GVHD prophylaxis across three pre-specified
comparisons.

## Methods

### Search strategy and selection criteria

This systematic review and meta-analysis was conducted in accordance
with PRISMA 2020 guidelines and registered with PROSPERO
(CRD420261372156). We searched EMBASE, PubMed, and SCOPUS from database
inception to April 30, 2026 for studies comparing PTCy-based GVHD
prophylaxis with alternative regimens in adult (≥18 years) allo-HSCT
recipients. The complete search strategy for PubMed is provided in the
[appendix (pp 2–4)](appendix-preview.html#s1.-search-strategy).
Reference lists of included studies and relevant reviews were
hand-searched. No language restrictions were applied at the search
stage; studies not available in English were excluded at full-text
review.

Studies were eligible if they reported at least one pre-specified
outcome with extractable event counts (numerator and denominator) for at
least two arms differing in GVHD prophylaxis strategy. Conference
abstracts were excluded. We defined three pre-specified comparisons: C1,
PTCy (with or without CNI or mycophenolate mofetil \[MMF\]) versus CNI
plus methotrexate (MTX) or MMF without ATG or T-cell depletion; C2, PTCy
versus ATG-based prophylaxis; and C3, within-PTCy regimen variants.

Two reviewers (MS and REL) screened titles and abstracts using the
Covidence platform (www.coevidence.org) and conducted data extraction
using a structured template ([appendix p
5](appendix-preview.html#s3.-characteristics-of-included-studies)).
AI-data tools (Claude Code, Anthropic, Inc.) was used to facilitate data
extraction from PDF source documents into the data collection form,
which were manually verified against source publications. Risk of bias
was assessed using ROBINS-I for observational studies and RoB 2 for
RCTs. Studies sharing patient cohorts were flagged and the most
comprehensive publication was designated as primary publication for each
cohort–outcome combination. All pooled estimates reported here were
derived from the from this cohort-deduplicated dataset, so that no
patient contributes more than once to any single outcome. The cohort
overlap map is provided in the [appendix (p
24)](appendix-preview.html#s12.-cohort-overlap).

### Outcomes

The primary outcome was overall survival (OS), analysed as all-cause
mortality (death as the event) at the reported timepoint. Secondary outcomes
included non-relapse mortality (NRM), acute GVHD grade II–IV (at day
+100), chronic GVHD (moderate to severe), CMV reactivation (any),
bloodstream infection (BSI, any pathogen), invasive fungal infection
(IFI, any), relapse-related mortality (RRM), BK virus reactivation, and
infection-related mortality (IRM).

### Statistical analysis

We fitted Bayesian random-effects binomial-logistic regression models
using `brms` (version 2.23.0) with an `rstan` backend in R (version
4.6.0). The primary model (M1) estimated the PTCy treatment effect
with a random intercept and a random PTCy-effect slope for study, so
that pooled effects average over between-study heterogeneity in the
treatment effect. Each study contributes a single row per outcome —
its preferred timepoint where reported (day +100 or +180 for early
outcomes, one year for late outcomes), otherwise the nearest reported
(fallback) timepoint — so no within-study correlation across
timepoints arises; an indicator variable distinguishes fallback from
preferred timepoints. Weakly informative priors were specified: N(0,
2·5) on fixed effects, N(0, 1·5) on the intercept, and Student t(3,
0, 1) on the between-study standard deviations (τ). Four chains of 4000
iterations (1000 warmup) were run with `adapt_delta` = 0·95 (increased
to 0·99 where divergent transitions occurred). Convergence was assessed
by R̂ and effective sample size. Single-arm descriptive studies
(n = 26) were retained for the PRISMA flow diagram and descriptive
tabulation only; because they report no comparator arm, they
contribute no outcome data to any comparative model, all of which
are restricted to studies reporting event counts for both a PTCy
and a non-PTCy arm. Arms receiving PTCy together with anti-thymocyte
globulin were classified as PTCy arms in all three comparisons; a
sensitivity analysis excluding the C2 studies containing such arms
is reported in appendix S9.

An exploratory steroid-adjustment model (M2), a post-hoc amendment
to the registered protocol (appendix S13), added arm-level systemic
corticosteroid exposure as a covariate. Because the covariate is
post-treatment and arm-level, and in most arms approximated from
acute GVHD incidence rather than directly reported, M2 estimates no
indirect effect and is reported only in the appendix (S9), together
with its definition, provenance, results, and a matched-set
comparison against M1.

Pre-specified sensitivity analyses included restriction to post-2020
publications (introduction of letermovir prophylaxis),
haploidentical-dominant cohorts (≥50% haploidentical donors), and
leave-one-out analysis. Hazard ratios were not pooled in the primary
analysis because most studies reported only event counts or
Kaplan–Meier estimates at fixed timepoints; in a post-hoc sensitivity
analysis, the reported overall-survival hazard ratios
(multivariable-adjusted where available, one per study, direction
harmonised to PTCy versus comparator with death as the event) were
pooled two-stage under a random-effects model (appendix S9).
Frequentist random-effects models (restricted
maximum likelihood \[REML\], `metafor` version 5.0.1) were fitted as
concordance checks. Publication bias was assessed using robust Bayesian
model-averaging (RoBMA). Certainty of evidence was assessed using the
GRADE framework adapted for observational evidence.

### Role of the funding source

There was no funding source for this study.

## Results

### Search results and study characteristics

The database search identified 4145 records (EMBASE 2603, PubMed 1061,
SCOPUS 481), of which 1220 were duplicates (@fig-prisma). After
screening 2925 titles and abstracts, 517 articles were sought for
full-text review; 52 could not be retrieved or were not in English. Of
465 full-text articles assessed, 214 were excluded ([appendix pp
6–14](appendix-preview.html#s2.-studies-excluded-at-full-text-screening-n214)),
leaving 251 studies for the systematic review. Of these, 106 unique
studies contributed outcome data to the meta-analysis across
three comparisons: C1 (73 studies), C2 (27 studies), and C3 (13
studies). Seven studies contribute to more than one comparison, so
the comparison counts sum to 113 rather than 106; the per-outcome
attrition from extraction to pooling is given in appendix S12.

The 225 comparative studies encompassed 520 arms and 177 758 patients
(@tbl-characteristics). Most were retrospective cohorts (132 \[59%\]) or
registry analyses (62 \[28%\]); 14 (6%) were RCTs. Median publication
year was 2023 (IQR 2021–24), with median follow-up of 26 months (IQR
20–36). PTCy arms were predominantly haploidentical donor transplants
(127 \[47%\]) whereas comparator arms were predominantly matched
unrelated (94 \[38%\]) or matched sibling (54 \[22%\]) donor
transplants.

### Risk of bias

Of 211 comparative observational studies assessed with ROBINS-I, 143
(68%) were at serious risk of bias and 68 (32%) at moderate risk,
primarily due to confounding by donor type and conditioning intensity;
no study was rated low or critical risk ([appendix pp
15–17](appendix-preview.html#s5.-risk-of-bias)). The 16 single-arm
descriptive studies were also rated but are not included in these
counts. Of 14 RCTs assessed
with RoB 2, 11 had some concerns (predominantly unblinded outcome
assessment), two were at high risk, and one was at low risk of bias.

### Comparison 1: PTCy versus CNI plus MTX or MMF

PTCy was associated with improved OS (k = 35, odds ratio 0·76 [95%
credible interval 0·62–0·93]; @fig-os). NRM showed a non-significant
trend toward benefit (k =
12, 0·81 \[0·46–1·22\]). Relapse-related mortality was lower (k = 34,
0·87 \[0·76–0·99\]).

Acute GVHD grade II–IV was substantially less frequent (k = 28, 0·58
\[0·44–0·77\]), as was moderate-to-severe chronic GVHD (k = 19, 0·40
\[0·22–0·68\]).

CMV reactivation was higher on average in the PTCy group, but the
credible interval included the null (k = 22, 1·22 [0·90–1·65];
@fig-cmv). The estimate was larger in post-2020 studies (k = 17, 1·46
[1·01–2·05]) and haploidentical-dominant cohorts (k = 12, 1·34
[0·90–1·96]). BSI estimates likewise favoured the comparator, with wide
intervals (k = 6, 1·42 [0·57–2·98]); no comparison-2 BSI model was
possible. BK virus reactivation showed the
largest infection effect, and the only one whose interval excluded the
null (k = 11, 2·39 [1·48–3·66]; @fig-infections). The IFI estimate was
highly uncertain in either direction (k = 6, 0·63 [0·19–2·62]), with
extreme between-study heterogeneity in the treatment effect (τ = 1·28).
Infection-related mortality showed no excess with PTCy versus CNI plus
MTX or MMF (k = 13, 1·03 \[0·68–1·49\]).

### Comparison 2: PTCy versus ATG

The OS estimate favoured PTCy versus ATG but with substantial
uncertainty (k = 9, odds ratio 0·75 \[0·42–1·31\]).
Acute GVHD was less frequent on average, with the interval just reaching the
null (k = 8, 0·51 \[0·24–1·02\]). NRM could not be assessed (k = 2).
Relapse-related mortality was lower, with the interval reaching the
null (k = 10, 0·78 \[0·55–1·02\]). CMV
reactivation did not differ between strategies (k = 12, 0·86
\[0·50–1·42\]), in contrast with the elevated C1 estimate.
Infection-related mortality did not differ (k = 7, 0·98 \[0·63–1·83\]).
BK virus reactivation was elevated versus ATG (k = 3, 2·49
\[1·09–6·03\]), the only infection estimate in C2 whose interval
excluded the null.

### Comparison 3: within-PTCy variants

No significant differences were detected between PTCy-based regimen
variants for any outcome (OS 0·92, NRM 0·51, acute GVHD 0·43, chronic
GVHD 0·53, relapse-related mortality 0·78; all credible intervals
crossed the null; k = 4–7 per outcome).

### Confounding and robustness analyses

Sensitivity analyses are reported in full in appendix S9. Within-study
donor-type imbalance was small (median between-arm difference in
haploidentical-donor percentage 0), a meta-regression on that
difference was null for every C1 outcome, and in donor-matched
subsets (difference ≤15 percentage points) the C1 overall-survival
estimate was, if anything, stronger (0·60 [0·44–0·80], k = 22). In
randomised-trials-only analyses (C1, k = 3–7 per outcome), estimates
for overall survival (0·79 [0·58–1·06]), chronic GVHD (0·31
[0·09–0·99]), NRM (0·84 [0·47–1·52]) and CMV (1·19 [0·54–3·59])
were compatible with the pooled results, but the acute GVHD
reduction was attenuated (0·92 [0·60–1·31], k = 6). Splitting C1
comparators by backbone showed the survival benefit concentrated
against CNI plus MTX (0·53 [0·33–0·79], k = 12) and absent against
CNI plus MMF (1·30 [0·76–2·29], k = 5). Restricting CMV to
clinically significant infection rather than any reactivation removed
the elevation (0·94 [0·49–1·71], k = 8). Adjustment for a
letermovir enrolment-era proxy did not change the CMV estimate (1·23
[0·90–1·66]).

### Certainty of evidence

GRADE certainty was very low for all rated outcomes (@tbl-results),
reassessed against the cohort-deduplicated random-effects estimates
with publication-bias analyses re-run on the deduplicated datasets
([appendix
S10–S11](appendix-preview.html#s11.-grade-certainty-of-evidence-profiles)).
Imprecision downgrades were applied to every outcome whose credible
interval includes the null (C1 NRM, C1 CMV, C1 BSI, C1 IFI, C2 OS, C2
acute GVHD, C2 CMV). C1 OS and C1 acute GVHD were downgraded for
publication bias: robust Bayesian model-averaging found strong evidence
of bias for both (BF~bias~ 18·6 and 14·0), with bias-adjusted estimates
that were essentially null (appendix S10).

## Discussion

This systematic review and meta-analysis encompassing 251 studies, 525
arms, and over 178 000 patients (approximately 111 500 unique
patients after cohort deduplication) provides a comprehensive
evaluation of
infection risks with PTCy-based GVHD prophylaxis. Its dual-comparator
design and simultaneous analysis of survival, GVHD, and infection
outcomes within a unified Bayesian framework enables a mechanistic
interpretation that has not been possible in prior single-comparison
reviews.

The survival and GVHD findings are consistent in direction across
comparators, although precision varies. PTCy was associated with less
acute GVHD grade II–IV versus CNI plus MTX or MMF (odds ratio 0·58;
from a median comparator-arm incidence of 33%, about 108 fewer cases
per 1000 patients) and versus ATG (0·51, with the interval just
reaching the null), with correspondingly lower chronic GVHD. Overall
survival was better versus CNI-based prophylaxis (0·76
\[0·62–0·93\]); against a median comparator-arm mortality of 35% this
corresponds to about 59 fewer deaths per 1000 patients — an odds
ratio is not a relative risk, and certainty is very low. Versus ATG
the estimate also favoured PTCy but was imprecise (0·75
\[0·42–1·31\]). These findings
align with and extend the BMT CTN 1703 RCT, which established the
superiority of PTCy in the matched-donor setting.[@bolanosmeade2023] The
present analysis is consistent with this advantage extending across
donor types, conditioning regimens, and geographic settings, although
the ATG comparison was underpowered relative to C1. Two robustness
findings temper the survival and GVHD conclusions: the acute GVHD
reduction was attenuated in the randomised-trials-only analysis (0·92
\[0·60–1·31\], k = 6; appendix S9), so its estimated magnitude rests
partly on observational comparisons, and the C1 survival benefit was
concentrated in comparisons against CNI-plus-MTX backbones (0·53
\[0·33–0·79\]) and absent against CNI-plus-MMF (1·30 \[0·76–2·29\]),
indicating that comparator mix contributes to the pooled estimate.

The central contribution of this analysis is the clarification of
apparently contradictory infection findings, where PTCy produces
opposite infection infection risks depending on the comparator. PTCy
administered on days +3 and +4 after transplant eliminates alloreactive
T cells (the intended GVHD-preventive effect)[@kanakry2013;
@wachsmuth2019], but simultaneously depletes the nascent
pathogen-specific T-cell repertoire (a collateral immunological
cost)[@zhao2022]. In C1, this T-cell depletion manifested as higher
average CMV reactivation (odds ratio 1·22 \[0·90–1·65\]) and BSI (1·42
\[0·57–2·98\]), although credible intervals for both included the null
(the BSI estimate rests on six studies, with no comparison-2 model
possible).

The survival benefit, in contrast, is biologically plausible as a
consequence of GVHD suppression: PTCy was associated with less acute
and chronic GVHD
(table 2), and GVHD and its treatment are leading drivers of
morbidity and non-relapse mortality after transplantation. An
exploratory steroid-adjustment analysis reported in the appendix
(S9) is compatible with — but cannot demonstrate — this
GVHD–steroid pathway, because it adjusts for a post-treatment,
arm-level covariate.

```{=html}
<!-- RESOLVED 2026-10-01: mediation language removed; M2 is exploratory
     steroid adjustment. Matched-set M1 (0.77 on the same 28 studies) shows the
     attenuation is attributable to the covariate, not the subset. Old TODO
     removed. -->
```

The C2 analysis provides a partial test of this framework. If CMV
excess were an intrinsic property of cyclophosphamide, it should
persist regardless of comparator. Instead, the CMV estimate versus ATG
was directionally opposite to the C1 estimate (C2 0·86 \[0·50–1·42\]
versus C1 1·22 \[0·90–1·65\]). A formal indirect comparison of the two
pooled effects is directionally consistent but does not resolve the
difference: the posterior ratio of the C1 and C2 odds ratios is 1·43
\[0·80–2·63\], with 89% posterior probability that the C1 effect is the
larger ([appendix S9](appendix-preview.html#s9.-sensitivity-analyses)).
The contrast is also indirect in a stronger sense: C1 and C2 enrol
different populations (predominantly haploidentical versus matched-donor
transplants), so comparator and population effects cannot be separated.
A formal meta-regression on comparator class, pooling the C1 and C2
CMV datasets (k = 33), gave the same answer as the indirect contrast
(ratio of odds ratios 0·71 \[0·41–1·20\] for C2 versus C1; appendix
S9): the C2 estimate (0·86 \[0·50–1·42\]) is compatible with parity
as well as with an intermediate position. The depletion-depth
ordering (CNI-based \< PTCy \< ATG) is therefore a hypothesis
compatible with the data, not a demonstrated hierarchy.

BK virus reactivation does not fit this pattern. The elevation was
essentially identical against both comparators (C1 2·39 \[1·48–3·66\];
C2 2·49 \[1·09–6·03\]; ratio of pooled effects 0·95 \[0·36–2·44\]), a
comparator-invariant pattern that is more consistent with a
cyclophosphamide-specific effect than with T-cell depletion depth —
and BK virus reactivation with haemorrhagic cystitis is a recognised
cyclophosphamide effect, so this signal argues for a PTCy-specific
rather than a class-wide depletion mechanism. The C2 estimate rests
on only three studies and remains prior-influenced, but the Bayesian
fit itself converged cleanly (R̂ \< 1·01, effective sample sizes above
3000, no divergences), so the imprecision reflects study count, not
non-convergence. The depletion-depth
interpretation should therefore be restricted to CMV, and even there
treated as hypothesis-generating.

Several limitations of this analysis warrant discussion. First, the
evidence base is predominantly observational, and no outcome exceeded
low certainty under GRADE assessment; all outcomes were rated very low
certainty. Selection bias, confounding by
donor type, and centre-level practice variation are inherent limitations
that cannot be fully addressed by meta-regression. Second,
infection outcome definitions
varied across studies (for example, any CMV reactivation versus
clinically significant CMV infection; any positive blood culture versus
BSI requiring intensive care), introducing measurement heterogeneity.
Third, the IFI estimate (odds ratio 0·63 \[0·19–2·62\]) rests on
extreme between-study heterogeneity in the treatment effect (τ = 1·28)
and is likely confounded by antifungal prophylaxis practices; it is
compatible with anything from a large reduction to a large increase.
Fourth, cohort deduplication removes the largest registry publications
from the seven affected outcomes where a smaller series reports the
same patients in more detail, so the pooled totals for survival and
chronic GVHD rest on fewer patients than the size of the review would
suggest; a per-outcome comparison of estimates before and after
deduplication is provided in appendix S12. Finally,
with two arms per study the random-effects model is just-identified at
study level, so for sparse outcomes (k ≤ 6) the priors contribute
materially to the estimated between-study standard deviation, and
credible intervals for those outcomes should be read as lower bounds on
the true uncertainty.

The within-PTCy comparison (C3) found no detectable differences between
regimen variants for any outcome. With k = 4–7 per outcome and wide
credible intervals, however, this is absence of evidence rather than
evidence of equivalence, and it should not be read as supporting
flexibility in dosing or backbone selection.

These findings have clinical implications. For centres already using
PTCy, the infection costs are best weighed in absolute terms: at the
median comparator-arm rates, the CMV odds ratio of 1·22 corresponds
to about 50 additional reactivations per 1000 patients (a relative
risk of about 1·10, not 1·22, at a 48% baseline) and the BK odds
ratio of 2·39 to about 134 additional reactivations per 1000 from a
13% baseline, while no elevation was detected for clinically
significant CMV infection (appendix S9). Whether these costs are
shared with ATG-based regimens is unresolved: the comparator-class
test did not resolve the C1–C2 difference (appendix S9). Clinical
strategies to mitigate these costs should target T-cell reconstitution
(adoptive T-cell therapies, letermovir prophylaxis, earlier
immunosuppression tapering) rather than PTCy avoidance. The larger CMV
estimate in post-2020 studies (odds ratio 1·46 \[1·01–2·05\]) is not
explained by letermovir-era practice: no arm in the post-2020 cohort
had letermovir use recorded, and most of these cohorts enrolled
before or across the letermovir era (appendix S9), so the reasons
for the trend remain unclear. For NRM,
optimising GVHD control remains a key strategy, as approaches towards
reducing GVHD severity and attendant steroid exposure should translate
into NRM benefit.

In conclusion, PTCy is associated with better overall survival and
less GVHD versus
CNI-based prophylaxis, with less certain benefit versus ATG. Infection
estimates pattern differently by pathogen: CMV estimates are
directionally
consistent with the depth of T-cell depletion without establishing it,
whereas BK virus elevation was comparator-invariant and appears
cyclophosphamide-specific. All infection estimates were imprecise and
these mechanistic readings are hypothesis-generating. Where present, these costs are best addressed
through strategies targeting immune reconstitution. The present analysis
provides a unified framework for interpreting the benefit–harm balance
of PTCy; given very low certainty of evidence throughout, its findings
are hypotheses for adequately powered randomised trials rather than a
basis for guideline recommendations.

REL, MS, and DPK developed the study protocol. REL and MS performed the
searches, data extraction, risk of bias assessment, and statistical
analysis, and wrote the first draft of the report. MS verified the
extracted data. DPK revised the manuscript. All authors had full access

## Data sharing

Individual study-level data extracted for this systematic review,
including the complete extraction database and analytic datasets, are
available on a public GitHub repository
<https://github.com/lewis-id-lab/ptcy-infection.git>. The manuscript
source, including the notebooks that generate every table and figure, is
available with a rendered version for review at
<https://lewis-id-lab.github.io/ptcy-infection/>. The study protocol is
registered with PROSPERO (CRD420261372156).

## Figures

![**Study selection (PRISMA 2020 flow diagram).** 4145 records were
identified from databases (EMBASE 2603, PubMed 1061, SCOPUS 481) and
1220 duplicates removed. 2925 records were screened and 2408 excluded at
title and abstract. 517 reports were sought for retrieval; 52 were not
retrieved or not in English. 465 full-text reports were assessed and 214
excluded ([appendix pp
6–14](appendix-preview.html#s2.-studies-excluded-at-full-text-screening-n214)).
251 studies were included in the systematic review; 106 unique
studies contributed outcome data to the meta-analysis (C1 73 studies;
C2 27 studies; C3 13 studies; 7 studies contribute to more than one
comparison).](figures/Figure1_PRISMA_flow_diagram){#fig-prisma}

![Comparison 1: PTCy vs CNI + MTX/MMF (k = 22, odds ratio 1·22
\[0·90–1·65\])](figures/Figure3a_CMV_C1_forest_setB){#fig-cmv-a}

![Comparison 2: PTCy vs ATG (k = 12, 0·86
\[0·50–1·42\])](figures/Figure3b_CMV_C2_forest_setB){#fig-cmv-b}

**Forest plots — CMV reactivation.** Individual study odds ratios for
any CMV reactivation, with the pooled Bayesian posterior median and 95%
credible interval. The CMV estimate is elevated against CNI-based
prophylaxis but not against ATG, directionally consistent with a
T-cell depletion-depth gradient, although both intervals include the
null and the formal comparator-class comparison is unresolved
(appendix S9).
:::

![**Forest plots — bacterial, fungal, and BK viral infection risk

and pooled Bayesian random-effects posterior median with 95% credible

pooled row. Panel A: bloodstream infection, any pathogen (k = 6, odds
ratio 1·42 \[0·57–2·98\]). Panel B: invasive fungal infection, any (k =
6, 0·63 \[0·19–2·62\]; τ = 1·28). Panel C: BK virus reactivation (k =
11, 2·39 \[1·48–3·66\]), the largest infection effect observed and the
only one whose interval excluded the null. All panels are comparison 1
